chapter_theme: The kaathai of the dream: as Puhar's women light the evening lamps, the poet tells how the god Pasanda Saathan once took a dead child from a desperate mother, gave her a child that was himself, grew up as a Brahmin youth, married Devanthi and left her for his temple; Devanthi, worshipping there, comes to bless Kannaki, hears her ominous dream of a great city, a false charge, a plea before the king and harm to the city, blames a vow broken in a former birth and urges bathing in the shore tanks, which Kannaki declines as unworthy; then Kovalan comes home ashamed of his lost wealth, takes her anklets as capital and leaves with her for Madurai before dawn, driven, the narrator says, by the deed at its term.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, alone in his house
the dancer Kovalan has left; named only in the closing venba
Kannaki's friend, a Brahmin woman whose husband was the god Saathan
a Brahmin's wife whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it
the god Saathan of the sects, who takes the form of a young woman, then of the dead child, and becomes Devanthi's husband
the corpse-eating demoness of the burning-ground shrine
a young serving woman of Kannaki's house

silappathikaram:9:1-28.reading: While the women of the inner city scatter jasmine buds and paddy and show the lamps at dusk, the poet goes back to an earlier day: Maalathi, whose co-wife's baby choked on the milk she gave it, fearing that the Brahmin and his wife would blame her unjustly, carried the child round every shrine of the city begging the gods to cure her grief and lay prostrate before Pasanda Saathan, who came as a young woman, told her that gods grant no boon to those without tapas, took the body to the burning-ground shrine where the corpse-eating demoness swallowed it, then, as she wept, bade her see her child alive and, becoming that child in a koel-haunted grove, put the magic child in its mother's hands.
silappathikaram:9:1-28.nuance: The catalogue of lines 9 to 13 takes Maalathi through the shrines of Indra's tree, the white elephant, the white Naga, the sun, the city, Vel, the thunderbolt, the god outside the town, the Nigantha (Jain) shrine and the moon: the city's gods stand side by side with no school set above another, and the one who answers is the god of the sects (பாசண்டம்). Saathan's rule (line 17) is stated and then exceeded by his own act: Maalathi has no tapas, he says, yet he gives her back a child, by becoming it. Her fear is of a false charge (படாதன, line 7), the same shape as the false word in Kannaki's dream later in this kaathai. Lines 1 to 4 belong to the frame of the whole kaathai: the tale of Saathan is told as a digression hung on மேல்ஓர்நாள்.
silappathikaram:9:1-28.event: Maalathi carries her co-wife's dead baby to every shrine; Saathan, as a young woman, gives the body to the burning-ground demoness and then returns to her as the child himself.

claims.claim: the gods grant no boon to those who have done no tapas

silappathikaram:9:1-28.unit_note: Boundary moved from 15|16 to 28|29, merging the old units 1-15 and 16-31's first part: line 15 (பாடு கிடந்தாளுக்கு,) is a dative that needs the speech of lines 16 to 19, and the miracle sentence closes in line 28 (தாய்கைக் கொடுத்தாள் அத் தையலாள்); line 29 (தூய மறையோன்பின் மாணியாய்) begins the child's life as a Brahmin youth.

silappathikaram:9:29-44.reading: The child grew up a Brahmin student, mastered the learning of the scriptures, and after the death of his foster-parents settled the inheritance with the kin and paid the rites owed to father and mothers; he married Devanthi, showed her his own ageless youth, told her to come to his shrine, and left; Devanthi, telling people her husband had gone to bathe at every holy ford and making that her pretext, keeps worship at the shrine to win him back, and now, sensing that Kannaki has a lack, comes scattering arugu, poolai flowers and paddy and blesses her to have her husband.
silappathikaram:9:29-44.nuance: Devanthi is a wife whose husband is a god, and she worships that god to have the husband back: the rival of Kannaki's way, where the husband is the only god (see the link to Kural 55). Her public story, that he has gone on pilgrimage to the fords (line 38), is a cover she lays on something (ஒன்றன் மேல் இட்டு, line 39), and the blessing she brings is the household rite of arugu and paddy, which Kannaki answers with a dream rather than thanks. That the god does the funeral and inheritance duties of a son (lines 30 to 32) makes his human life complete before he leaves it.
silappathikaram:9:29-44.event: Saathan, grown as a Brahmin, marries Devanthi, reveals himself and leaves; Devanthi worships at his shrine and comes to bless Kannaki.
silappathikaram:9:29-44.unit_note: Boundaries moved from 31|32 and 47|48 to 28|29 and 44|45: line 29 begins the child's grown life, and line 44 closes Devanthi's blessing (பெறுக கணவனோடு என்றாள்) before Kannaki's reply begins; the one word பெறுகேன் at the end of line 44 opens her answer and is read with the next unit.

silappathikaram:9:45-54.reading: Kannaki answers that she will have him, but that her heart is shaking from a dream: he took her hand, they went into a great city, the people there laid on him a word that did not belong to him, as one drops a scorpion, a harm befell Kovalan, she made a plea before the king, and with the king there was a harm to the city too, of which she will not speak; it is like an evil omen, she says, and if her friend heard the good that came to her with the one she had joined, she would laugh.
silappathikaram:9:45-54.nuance: The dream is the poem's plot in small, told before the journey begins: city, false charge, harm to Kovalan, her plea before the king, the city's harm, and a last good that sounds absurd. She refuses to tell the city's harm (உரையாடேன், line 51), and the final good is told only as something that would be laughed at; the poem's later units show both. The scorpion image (இடுதேள், line 48) makes the charge something thrown on, not earned. Lines 51 to 54 are dense, and which of the repeated உற்ற forms refers to Kovalan and which to the 'harm' is not certain.
silappathikaram:9:45-54.event: Kannaki tells Devanthi a dream of a false charge on Kovalan in a great city, her plea before the king and harm to the city.
silappathikaram:9:45-54.unit_note: Unit runs 45-54, from the start of Kannaki's dream (கடுக்கும்என் நெஞ்சம் கனவினால்) to the end of her speech in line 54 (நகைஆகும்); the old boundary 47|48 split the dream mid-sentence.

silappathikaram:9:55-66.reading: Devanthi answers that Kannaki is not one who has failed her husband in this life, but in a former birth she broke a vow to him, and bids that fault be gone; on the shore grove where the sea and the Kaveri meet there are two tanks, the Moon's and the Sun's, and women who bathe there and worship at the shrine of Kama enjoy their husbands in this world and are born again in the land of enjoyment, so let them bathe one day; Kannaki says it is not worthy and sits on, and then a young serving woman announces that Kovalan has come to the gate.
silappathikaram:9:55-66.nuance: Devanthi gives a cause for Kannaki's lack, a vow broken in a former birth, and the remedy of a rite; the poem later gives another cause, a curse on Kovalan's own former birth told by the goddess of Madurai (Silappathikaram 23), and does not take up Devanthi's. Kannaki's பீடு அன்று (line 64) refuses the rite for herself without disputing its power: she does not say the tanks fail, only that seeking a husband through Kama's shrine is beneath her, which the poem's later venba turns into a wife whom the gods worship. போகம்செய் பூமி is a land of enjoyment where the next birth is spent; the term is at home in Jain cosmology, but the unit does not tie it to a school. Line 55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) is obscure; I read it as 'you have not wronged him (in this life)', and other readings are possible.
silappathikaram:9:55-66.event: Devanthi urges Kannaki to bathe in the shore tanks and worship at Kama's shrine; Kannaki refuses, and a maid announces Kovalan's return.

claims.claim: a vow to her husband broken in a former birth causes a wife's present lack
women who bathe in the Soma and Surya tanks and worship at Kama's shrine enjoy their husbands here and are reborn in the land of enjoyment

silappathikaram:9:55-66.unit_note: Unit runs 55-66 (the old unit 48-66 less its first seven lines, which go with Kannaki's dream): it opens with Devanthi's reply (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) and ends, as before, with the maid's announcement in line 66.

silappathikaram:9:67-79.reading: Kovalan enters the bedchamber, sees her wasted body and her pain, and says that having sported with a deceiver of deceitful ways, the poverty of losing the mountain of wealth his family gave him shames him; with a bright smile she offers the anklets, and he answers that with the anklets as his beginning he will earn back the wealth that is gone, and bids her rise and go with him to Madurai; driven by the deed at its term, he sets out before the night's dark is cleared.
silappathikaram:9:67-79.nuance: Kovalan blames Madhavi (சலதி, line 69) and names his own feeling as shame at poverty, not remorse toward Kannaki; she answers with no word of reproach, only the anklets. His plan is an ordinary remedy, to trade and recover; the narrator's last line gives the plan another author, the deed that drives him to its term (வினைகடைக் கூட்ட, line 78). The anklet enters the story here as capital (சிலம்பு முதலாக, line 74), the thing that will become the charge in the dream.
silappathikaram:9:67-79.event: Kovalan returns ashamed of his lost wealth, takes Kannaki's offered anklets as capital and leaves with her for Madurai before dawn.

claims.claim: a past deed at its term drives a man to the place of its fruit
losing inherited wealth to a deceitful courtesan brings a man shame

silappathikaram:9:80-83.reading: The closing venba says that, as the dream his beloved saw and Madhavi's word came to nothing, the deed of old driving him to its end, he set out before the night's dark was cleared.
silappathikaram:9:80-83.nuance: The venba puts the old deed (மூதை வினை) where the kaathai's last line had only வினை. What 'made Madhavi's word empty' means is not certain: it may be Madhavi's word sent to Kovalan in the preceding kaathai, now come to nothing because he has left with Kannaki; the syntax of காதலி கண்ட கனவு beside it is also open.
silappathikaram:9:80-83.event: Kovalan sets out from Puhar before dawn.

claims.claim: an old deed drives its doer to his end

links.note: Saathan's rule that gods grant no boon without tapas uses the couplet's own word செய்தவம், and then he grants Maalathi a child she has not earned.
links.teaches: Read with the couplet, the tale shows that the rule linking tapas to its reward is the god's to state and also the god's to override, so grace in the epic stands beside the merit rule rather than inside it.

gains.a: the general law behind Saathan's line 17, which shows his gift to Maalathi as an exception to it
gains.b: a scene where the law is spoken by a god to a woman without tapas and then not applied

links.note: Saathan says gods give no boon to those without tapas; the goddess of Madurai later says that when a former deed comes in wrath, tapas does not help those not upright.
links.teaches: Together the two divine sayings set limits on tapas from both sides: without it no boon, and with it no shield once an old deed has ripened against one who was not upright.

links.note: Devanthi, whose husband is a god, keeps worship at his shrine to have him back; the couplet sets worship of a god against worship of a husband.
links.teaches: Devanthi's case dissolves the couplet's either-or, since her god is her husband, and so throws Kannaki's refusal of the shrine in the next unit into relief as a choice the couplet's terms describe exactly.

gains.a: a measure for Devanthi's piety as the reverse of the couplet's wife, which prepares the contrast with Kannaki
gains.b: a case the couplet did not foresee, a wife whose husband is himself the god she worships

links.note: The dream's plea before the king (காவலன் முன்னர் யான் கட்டுரைத்தேன்) is fulfilled when Kannaki stands before the Pandya and argues her case.
links.teaches: Set beside the plea, the dream shows that Kannaki's speech before the king was foreseen as her own act from the start, not a chance turn of grief, and that she already knew it would bring harm to the city.

links.note: The 'good' that would be laughed at if told is the ending in which Kannaki, after fourteen days, rises to heaven with Kovalan.
links.teaches: The pairing explains why Kannaki calls the dream's ending laughable: a reunion that comes only after death and in the form of gods sounds absurd as a blessing to a living wife.

links.note: Offered bathing and Kama's shrine as a way to keep her husband, Kannaki says it is not worthy; the couplet praises the wife who worships her husband rather than a god.
links.teaches: The scene shows the couplet's wife as one who refuses a rite offered for her own good, at the cost of the remedy, and that the refusal is framed as dignity (பீடு), not as doubt about the gods.

gains.a: the rule that explains Kannaki's refusal without making her a sceptic about the tanks
gains.b: a lived test in which the wife turns down divine help for her marriage at the moment she most needs it

links.note: Devanthi blames a vow Kannaki broke to her husband in a former birth; the goddess of Madurai later traces the disaster to a curse on Kovalan's former self, who had Sangaman killed.
links.teaches: The poem offers two former-birth causes for the same ruin and gives the authoritative one to a goddess, so the friend's guess that the fault was the wife's own is left standing as a mistaken reading.

links.note: Kannaki declines to worship at Kama's shrine for her husband; the Katturai venba says the gods themselves worship her who worships her husband and no god.
links.teaches: The early refusal and the later venba make one arc: the wife who would not seek her husband through a god ends as one the gods receive, so the poem pays out the refusal in the Kural's own terms.

links.note: Kovalan devises a remedy for his ruin, to trade with the anklets in Madurai, and in the same line the narrator says the deed was driving him; the couplet says fate gets there first even when one plans another way.
links.teaches: The pairing shows fate overtaking a plan by using the plan itself: Kovalan's scheme to recover is the very road by which the deed reaches him, a case the couplet's bare 'it gets there first' does not picture.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the narrator credits Kovalan's sensible plan to the deed (line 78)
gains.b: a concrete mechanism: the counter-plan becomes fate's vehicle rather than being outrun by it

links.note: Kovalan blames a deceitful woman for the poverty that shames him; the couplet ranks double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of those Fortune has left.
links.teaches: Kovalan speaks the couplet's judgment of himself, but the closing venba and the narrator put his ruin down to the old deed, so the epic lets the Kural's verdict on courtesans stand as a ruined man's account rather than as the cause.

gains.a: a standard of the age against which Kovalan's blame of Madhavi sounds conventional and self-excusing
gains.b: a speaker who applies it to himself in the moment of loss, while the story he is in names another cause

links.note: The venba says the old deed drove Kovalan out of Puhar before dawn; the quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
links.teaches: In the quatrain the deed seeks the doer; in the venba the doer is moved toward the deed, so together they show karma working from both ends, the deed seeking and the doer being sent.

gains.a: an image for why the venba gives the deed the active verb கடைக்கூட்ட
gains.b: a narrative case where the search ends by bringing the doer to a distant city, not by the deed arriving at his door

links.note: The venba's மூதை வினை is unnamed here; the goddess of Madurai later names it as the curse of Sangaman's widow on Kovalan's former self.
links.teaches: Read together, the venba sets the deed moving with no content and the later speech fills it in, so the departure from Puhar is the first step of a debt whose terms the reader learns only after the death.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: The kaathai has 83 lines but the edition's printed last line number is 75 (`show`: 'printed last line 75'); line numbers here are `show`'s 1 to 83.
Line 28 carries a repaired encoding flag (TSCII leftover read as ூ in தூய); the repaired reading fits the sense.

Lines 82-83 of the closing venba repeat lines 78-79 word for word (வினைகடைக் கூட்ட வியம்கொண்டான் கங்குல் / கனைசுடர் கால்சீயா முன்); this looks like the venba's deliberate echo of the kaathai's last lines, not a doubling, but it is recorded.
Line 55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) and lines 51-54 (தீக்குற்றம் போலும் ... நகைஆகும்) are obscure in wording; the readings of those units are marked uncertain.
